notes: \cpara{A note to the blog's readers, written at the AGI-08 conference. The ``mathy posts'' are the preceding posts on entropy, mutual information and Naive Bayes.}
\cpara{Sets up the example: a hotel with triangular lightbulbs.}
\cpara{Asks the reader to picture the bulb before reading on.}
\cpara{Reports the author's own image, offered as ``as best as my introspection could determine'': a sharp pyramid, then smoothed edges, then a triangular fluorescent loop.}
\cpara{Draws the point of the example, again hedged (``As far as I can tell''): the image was revised without words.}

\cpara{Describes the imagery debate. Its two sides are usually identified with Stephen Kosslyn, for picture-like images, and Zenon Pylyshyn, for whom the representations are ``propositional, language-like, symbolic'' (Pearson and Kosslyn, \textsc{PNAS}, 2015). The ``LISP token'' is a fair short name for the second view.}

\cpara{The post names the hindsight effect and then gives the verdict anyway. Three paragraphs later it grants that the question ``used to be harder to answer, back in the day of the controversy.'' Introspection did not settle it either: in a study reported by the \textsc{Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy} (Reisberg 2003), researchers with less vivid imagery were more likely to take the propositional side.}

\cpara{Offered with ``I think,'' and the sources point the other way. The propositional side posited ``symbolic internal representations'' (Pearson and Kosslyn 2015). Traditional behaviorism, in the \textsc{Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy}'s words, ``tried to free psychology from having to theorize about how animals and persons represent (internally, in the head) their environment.'' The same encyclopedia's entry on mental imagery says it was this debate that made philosophers take imagery seriously again, ``after a long period of behaviorist-inspired skepticism about anything imagery-related.''}

\cfact{Overstated for the best-known behaviorist. Of B.~F. Skinner the \textsc{Stanford Encyclopedia} (``Behaviorism'') says: ``He readily admits that private thoughts and so on exist.'' Skinner treated them as inner behavior, to be described in the same terms as outward behavior.}
\cpara{Raises the obvious objection: is the evidence only that you can close your eyes and see images?}

\cpara{Gives the classic evidence, correctly. This is Shepard and Metzler's mental-rotation experiment (\textsc{Science}, 1971), whose abstract reports times that are ``a linearly increasing function of the angular difference'' between the two drawings.}

\cpara{The post's side is the one the \textsc{Stanford Encyclopedia}'s current entry favors. It reports that visualizing a triangle produces ``a roughly triangle-pattern activation'' in primary visual cortex, and that many researchers have ``declared this debate dead.'' But it was not settled when the post was written. In 2003 Pylyshyn argued that the evidence from neural imaging ``does little to justify this recidivism because it does not address the format of mental images'' (\textsc{Trends in Cognitive Sciences}). The post cites one side's book, whose subtitle announces the resolution; in 2015 Kosslyn co-wrote a paper subtitled ``Ending the imagery debate.''}
\cpara{Turns to the thesis, with a hedge (``Part of the reason''): people misuse words because they underrate what lies behind them.}
\cpara{Says the letters of ``apple'' are only a small visible part of the word.}
\cpara{The title's image: the concepts behind words can draw pictures in one's own mind and, through shared labels, in someone else's.}

\cfact{Not everyone can, to the same degree. Differences in the vividness of imagery have been known since Galton (1880), and some people report no conscious imagery at all, a condition named aphantasia in 2015 (\textsc{Stanford Encyclopedia}, ``Mental Imagery''). The post's own list of what the apple concept does, two paragraphs on, includes recognizing and tasting, which need no picture.}
\cpara{Argues that the letters cannot carry the picture: ``Apple'' is 5 bytes, and a picture needs more data.}
\cpara{Lists what the concept behind the tag can do: draw a picture, combine with other concepts, recognize, taste, act.}
\cpara{Argues that imagery is not mere recall, since one can picture things never seen, such as a triangular lightbulb.}
\cpara{States the conclusion in programming terms: a word is a pointer, and at some point it must be dereferenced.}
